newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: E. Timor leader says only Suharto blocks change.
newsitem.headline: E. Timor leader says only Suharto blocks change.

text.p: East Timorese independence leader Jose Ramos Horta, co-winner of the 1996 Nobel peace prize, said on Tuesday Indonesian President Suharto was the only impediment to change in East Timor and Indonesia itself.
"He is the only one still alive today in office who was involved in the initial invasion of East Timor," Horta told reporters after a meeting with Secretary-General Kofi Annan.
It was the first time in 22 years that a U.N. chief had agreed to meet an East Timorese representative, he added.
"I believe the only impediment today to changes in Indonesia and East Timor is President Suharto himself," said Horta, a long-time campaigner for self-determination.

Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 after Portugal withdrew from its former colony, which Indonesia annexed the following year as its 27th province. Guerrillas of the Fretilin independence movement continued for years to mount attacks on Indonesian troops.

The international community does not recognise the annexation, and talks under U.N. auspices between the foreign ministers of Portugal and Indonesia aimed at finding an acceptable solution have dragged on since 1983.

Horta said whoever came after Suharto, even a military figure, would have a "golden opportunity ... to easily say, 'Yes, it's not my responsibility. Let's change.' Because the costs are becoming bigger and bigger for Indonesia."
Change could even come from Suharto himself, Horta said, citing the example of such leaders as South African President F.W. de Klerk and Mikhail Gorbachev in the former Soviet Union.
"Even with Suharto, we hope that with divine inspiration coupled with some pragramtism, a sense of realism, he can reverse course," he said.

Replying to questions, Horta criticised the Geneva-based U.N. Human Rights Commission for a "total lack of will ... to address seriously the growing human rights problems in East Timor and in Indonesia itself."
If the commission, for the fifth year in a row, adopted a so-called chairman's statement instead of a strongly worded resolution, it would amount to "an evasion of responsibilities."
Horta said he told Annan of his "total willingness" to cooperate with him and his staff to find a just, comprehensive and internationally acceptable solution to the East Timor problem.

He also promised to be flexible and to "try to understand Indonesia's own sensitivities and good name" and not to exacerbate the situation. But he would also be "very firm on the issue of self-determination."
He expressed gratitude to the secretary-general for having recently named a personal representative for East Timor, for the first time in more than 20 years.

Horta said the envoy, former Pakistani U.N. ambassador Jamsheed Marker, had already visited Portugal and would shortly travel to Indonesia and East Timor. He hoped Marker would also be able to meet Fretilin leader Xanana Gusmao, captured by Indonesia in November 1992 and jailed for 20 years.
